title: Only a Little While
author: Frau Erica
summary: The *Sängerbote* of February 15, 1913 — Volume 1, Number 1 — included a five-verse hymn text by Adelheid Rickmeyer Mueller (Frau Erica). Frau Erica's granddaughter Adelheid Mueller Nickel, who inherited the bound *Sängerbote* volume, tucked a note into the book on page 4, suggesting that Frau Erica evidently thought she was nearing the end of her life. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=745).

title: My Songs
author: Frau Erica
summary: Frau Erica discusses her approach to song-writing. There is a bit of self-effacing commentary, where she observes that some of her songs are somewhat plain (wearing simple clothes) and could be dismissed by sophisticates of the time for being out of date. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=746).

title: My Last Greeting
author: Frau Erica
summary: With the Muellers (including Wilhelm, her fiancé) already in Indiana, Frau Erica emigrated alone as a 22-year-old woman — a courageous step in 1867. This ran in the inaugural issue of the *Sängerbote*, February 1913. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=746).

title: Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread
author: Frau Erica
summary: It is not clear whether this reverie on a petition in the Lord's Prayer was an original composition by Frau Erica or was a piece of work she admired. *Mitgeteilt* could mean contributed, sent to us, discovered or some other kind of agency. Most of Frau Erica's writings are signed simply "Erica." [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=748).

title: The Cultivation of Music and Singing in Christian Family Circles
author: Frau Erica
summary: In a longer essay, Frau Erica discusses the importance of music in the home, particularly as a necessary element in childrearing, and the value of music in the home for supporting congregational singing everywhere. [View the original *Sängerbote* pages](/galleries/33?image=749) (the essay runs across two pages of the November 1913 issue).

title: On Golgatha
author: Frau Erica
summary: The *Sängerbote* featured devotional writing, a reflection both of its audience and of the times. That suited Frau Erica quite well. She continued writing devotional poetry throughout her life. (Her final piece, *"Wenn Wir Keinen Heiland Hätten,"* appeared in the [*Stadtmissionar*](/documents/79). The editors described it as *"fragmentärisch."*) Note how Frau Erica used letter spacing to emphasize *"nichts"* in the second verse. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=751).

title: God’s Messengers
author: Frau Erica
summary: A handwritten note in the *Sängerbote* suggested that Frau Erica composed this piece as a commentary on the work of her two sons who became ordained Lutheran ministers. It appeared in August 1914 (Vol. 2, Nr. 7). [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=752).

title: About My Child
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: Opa – Rev. Ernst Heinrich Constantine Mueller – would have been about 40 years old when his fourth son Herbert was born (February 6, 1914). This four-stanza verse appeared in the ninth issue of *Sängerbote*, a few days after Herbert's first birthday. Herbert's son Robert, a composer and music faculty member at the University of Arkansas, composed a musical setting 80 years later. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=753).

title: A Country Pastor Longs for Spring
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: An interesting moment in the life of a rural pastor — late winter weariness and frustration eased by promises of spring and restoration. The double capital in "HErrn," apparently intentional, is original to the *Sängerbote*. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=754).

title: Greenbriar’s Captain
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: Ernst Mueller's poem of war, neutrality, and flags aboard the Greenbriar ran in the May 15, 1915, edition. On April 12, 1915, the Greenbriar struck a mine and sank about 47 miles outside Bremerhaven while under control of a German captain. The first full account of the loss appeared in the New York Times on April 24, 1915. It is possible, although highly unlikely, that news of the Greenbriar's demise had reached rural southern Minnesota in time for the May issue. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=755).

title: Gold for Iron?
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: Although they never set foot in Germany, Ernst (Opa) Mueller and his sister Dora were of the first American-born immigrant generation, raised to admire both countries. The Great War had become a costly stalemate of trenches; America had not yet entered the conflict. Ernst wrote that he would give money (gold) to support German widows and orphans, but his allegiance now belonged to America, the only nation for which he would bear arms (*Eisen*/iron). Dora, on the other hand, had implored the Lord's blessing on the German army in her own *Mein Vaterland*, elsewhere in the *Sängerbote*. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=757).

title: Victory
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: Rev. Ernst Mueller worked a number of themes into four verses: horrors of war, a hint of pacifism, an observation that the Germans and their enemy were both serving their fatherlands, death as victory, and, as America pondered entry to WWI, pointing out that the young German's death came from a bullet of American steel. This appeared in the *Sängerbote* of February 1916. (*Feldgraue* was also used as a term for German army uniforms — battlefield gray — and a suggestion of battle fatigue is also appropriate.) [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=758).

title: For the Singing Contest 1917
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: A difficult dual thematic writing task for 1917: World War One and the upcoming 400th anniversary of the Lutheran Reformation. Ernst Mueller focused on the power of the Word — the *Hier stehe ich* moment in Luther's presentation at the Diet of Worms (April 1521) — and on the guidebook (the "Enchiridion") that was Luther's Catechism. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=760).

title: A People United
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: A strange claim for Martin Luther: Otto von Bismarck was having some success in war with a united German populace. Author Ernst Mueller points out that it was Luther, not Bismarck, who brought a unifying language to Germany. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=760).

title: Minneopa
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: Minneopa, from the Dakota language for "water falling twice," became Minnesota's third state park in 1905. Since the mid-1800's, visitors had traveled by train or up the Minnesota River by paddleboat to hike and view the double falls. As children and later in adulthood, the Muellers often visited Minneopa for *Speck und Eier,* a hearty picnic breakfast of bacon and eggs. Ernst Mueller's poem appeared in the May 1916 edition of *Sängerbote*. His daughter Adelheid astonished her college lit class by reciting it from memory about a decade later. In 1924, when the little brook at Minneopa had run dry, Ernst wrote a [short sequel](/documents/286). [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=761).

title: Minneopa in 1924
author: Ernst Mueller
summary: At some point, likely in the early 1920s, the brook at Minneopa ran dry. Ernst Mueller wrote a small sequel to the original ["Minneopa,"](/documents/284) although it was never published in the *Sängerbote* or elsewhere. His daughter Adelheid transcribed the sequel, written by Opa in beautiful German script, and attempted a translation. [View the manuscript](/galleries/33?image=762).

title: Latin Church Hymns
author: Fred Knief
summary: Friedrich Knief was the first child of Theodora Mueller, eldest of the nine original Mueller immigrant children, and the Rev. Ludwig Knief. Friedrich and his wife Dora Mueller, first cousins, were writers and editors for German periodicals in Milwaukee. Fred contributed longer essays and a humorous piece to the *Sängerbote*. He also wrote a brief history of the Mueller family in America and edited his father's *Lebenslauf* (autobiography). [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=763).

title: Michelangelo as Poet
author: Fred Knief
summary: Friedrich Knief, son of a Lutheran minister, was well-schooled in the teachings of Martin Luther, particularly the *sola gratia* part. In Michelangelo's sonnets, written late in life, Knief found evidence that Michelangelo recognized grace rather than good works as the essential key, an insight Knief explored in a later essay on the poet [Vittoria Colonna](/documents/292). [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=765).

title: Vittoria Colonna
author: Fred Knief
summary: Friedrich Knief's essay on [Michelangelo as poet](/documents/290) (*Sängerbote* No. 7, August 1914) explored a significant theological insight that the elder Michelangelo developed through friendship and correspondence with the poet Vittoria Colonna. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=768).

title: The Glorious!
author: Fred Knief
summary: Fred Knief — Friedrich Constantinus Knief — contributed some longer essays to the *Sängerbote*, including this humorous encounter with a player piano in a Milwaukee department store. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=771).

title: Behold, Zion, Your God Is King
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The regular meter and dependable rhyme scheme (A-B, A-B, C-C) suggest this is a six-verse hymn. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=752).

title: Evening Bells
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The anticipation of and longing for heaven was a frequent theme for Dora. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=753).

title: My Heart Wants to Sing and Blossom
author: Dodo Knief
summary: A theme that complements her earlier “An meinen Gatten.” [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=753).

title: He Will Be Your Comforter
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The *Sängerbote* of August 1913 (Volume 1, Number 3) had a group of five pieces by Dora Knief, of which this was the lead item. Frau Erica and Dora Knief were the only Mueller-family authors in volume one. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=772).

title: My Song
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dora Elizabeth Mueller and Friedrich Constantinus Knief, husband and wife, were also first cousins, married by Ludwig Knief February 28, 1899, in Klinger, Iowa. They were writers and editors in Milwaukee until 1923, when Fred and Dodo moved their family to Santa Monica, California. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=772).

title: Bridesmaid’s Song
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The first of two hymns Dora wrote for her brother Paul's wedding June 3, 1909. A note in the text says it can be sung to the melody “So nimm denn meine Hände.” [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=772).

title: Wedding Song
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dodo and Fred Knief helped host [the wedding](/documents/247) of Dodo's brother Paul G. Mueller and Henrietta Strelow on June 3, 1909, in Milwaukee. An introductory note says the German text was fitted to the English hymn tune “Dreams of Paradise.” [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=772).

title: The Little Church in the Forest
author: Dodo Knief
summary: A celebration of small-church authenticity and a dismissal of cathedral-sized church affairs. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=773).

title: I Am So Homesick
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The first of two poems on page 89 of the *Sängerbote* that deal with an intense spiritual longing for eternal life. The two works were written nearly a decade apart — this one in September 1913, the [other](/documents/314) in 1904. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=774).

title: The Longing that Is Never Silent
author: Dodo Knief
summary: An unusual discussion of the spiritual longing for eternal life, which transcends even the intimacy of the family circle. Dora wrote this in 1904 either before or after the birth of her son Paul in September. Her daughter Gretchen would have been three. She [revisited](/documents/312) the theme almost a decade later. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=774).

title: Be welcomed by me, O Jesus
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dora Mueller Knief's Christmas carol, set to music by Walter Wismar, was published and circulated in November 1913, the first Christmas issue of the *Sängerbote*. It appears to be the only Mueller contribution distributed in sheet music format, and it includes her full name (with umlaut). [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=775).

title: Isaiah 43:1
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Evidently — but not explicitly — a bedside encouragement for a terminally ill or aged patient: “Zag' nicht! es währt nicht lange / Fear not! It will not last long.” [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=776).

title: But Guard Your Soul
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Much more than mere encouragement to keep smiling in adversity, the poem argues that giving in to anger, sorrow and resentment may well cause irreparable damage to the human soul. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=776).

title: On My Husband
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dodo wrote this for Fred in celebration of their 15th wedding anniversary. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=777).

title: As Long as in Your Soul
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Doubtful whispers, gossip, hateful tidings, even poisons from the evil tongue of a trusted friend — Dora has encountered them all, but they do not matter to those who can hear and listen to the voice of a pure heart. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=778).

title: A Poet’s Dedication
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The sensations and emotional complexities that stimulate creative poetry and music are recognizable but difficult to define or describe. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=779).

title: For Me!
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Three of Dora's verses begin with *für mich* (for me), expressions of gratitude and thanks for the gift of faith and the possibilities it offers. The last three verses begin with *für dich* (for you), addressed to the Lord and asking for divine support of earnest efforts on behalf of the kingdom of God on Earth. The first line of each three-verse set uses double spacing, an emphasis technique akin to italics. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=781).

title: Sing Me Your Song
author: Dodo Knief
summary: A plea for understanding and support at a difficult time — sing me your song — concludes with the observation that singing the song will also fill the heart of the singer with comfort. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=782).

title: The Power Is Yours
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Archduke Ferdinand was assassinated on June 28, 1914. A month later, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, followed by Germany on Russia, then France and Britain on Germany and Austria-Hungary. The world was at war when the November *Sängerbote* brought this piece from Dora Knief to its German immigrant readership. A lithograph on the facing page depicts a lone soldier standing in the snow with the title *“Er denkt an Weib und Kinder — vereinsamt und allein.”* [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=783).

title: My Fatherland
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dora was of the first American-born generation, as was her brother Ernst Mueller. Although neither had been to Germany, both wrote about the Fatherland as The Great War was underway. (See Ernst's [*Gold für Eisen?*](/documents/276).) [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=785).

title: Secrecy
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dora's point in the last verse is difficult to understand, as if she will never again sing of love because a confidence has been betrayed. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=786).

title: The Final Refuge
author: Dodo Knief
summary: A few chance remarks from family members of Dora and her brother Ernst's generation suggested that Dora and Ernst did not care much for each other. The first verse of this poem seems to support that observation. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=787).

title: I know, I will also carry further
author: Dodo Knief
summary: This five-verse poem initially seems like a rumination on lost love but develops into a complex story of love, death, bereavement, and loneliness. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=788).

title: Song of Joy
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Joy, like love — feelings internal to the heart — was a frequent topic for Dora. She tried often to understand it, to learn how it develops, to analyze what it can do, to ask whether it can be shared. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=789).

title: I would like one more thing
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Possibly an extension of the previous [*“Lied der Freudenschaft,”*](/documents/342) Dora figuratively takes happiness into her own hands. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=789).

title: The Restless Heart
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The first four verses discuss the restless heart — twitching and trembling at the slightest provocation. The last two verses speak of the poor or pitiable heart (Du armes Herz). [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=790).

title: Comfort for the Sick
author: Dodo Knief
summary: An unusual bedside reverie for a sick child (possibly one of Dora's own), urging courage in the face of suffering. Dora assures the child, *“Ich bin bei dir, auch in der Dunkelheit* / I am with you, even in the darkness.” [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=791).

title: The Child of War
author: Dodo Knief
summary: This was the first of three poems by Dora Mueller Knief in the September 1916 *Sängerbote*. (The fourth issue of the year normally ran in November.) [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=792).

title: Please
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Dora Knief, by far the most prolific of the Mueller contributors to the *Sängerbote*, writes about the poetic ability she recognizes as a gift from God and pleads for time to complete the creative work she has undertaken. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=792).

title: Solitude
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The last of Dora Knief's three poems on page 531 of the September 1916 *Sängerbote*. *Einsamkeit* is usually translated as loneliness, but that is not an experience anyone would want to seek or hope to find. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=792).

title: Johann Sebastian Bach (Part One)
author: Dodo Knief
summary: The Frau Erica archive does not have much information about Dora and Friedrich Knief, but Dora's extensive two-part essay on J.S. Bach suggests a lifelong musical awareness and training that began in childhood. See her mother Frau Erica's *Sängerbote* piece on the cultivation of music ([*Die Pflege der Musik*](/documents/264)) within the family circle. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=793).

title: Johann Sebastian Bach (Part Two)
author: Dodo Knief
summary: In the concluding half of her essay on Johann Sebastian Bach, Dora Knief sets Bach as a creative figure in a place well beyond Germany and Europe. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=798).

title: Fellow Hikers
author: Dodo Knief
summary: For her final three-poem set in the bound *Sängerbote*, Dora Knief examines the human relationship with the natural world — which is, for the most part, supportive of life's remaining journey. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=803).

title: Greeting
author: Dodo Knief
summary: Experiencing the Earth — walking, hiking, listening, viewing — supports human relationships no matter how distant. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=803).

title: “The Longing Song of One’s Own Heart”
author: Dodo Knief
summary: In her last poem of the bound *Sängerbote*, Dora Knief observes that although the Earth does not respond emotionally to sadness or happiness, it does reflect the thoughts and moods of a person's own heart. [View the original *Sängerbote* page](/galleries/33?image=803).

title: Stars and Stripes
author: O.F. Meissner
summary: The *Sängerbote*'s *Amerikanische Vaterlandslieder* section led with O.F. Meissner's singable German text for the Star-Spangled Banner — this less than a year before the United States entered The Great War. The song was broadly popular long before Meissner's version appeared here; Meissner set three stanzas, where Francis Scott Key had originally composed four. The song wasn't yet the national anthem — Woodrow Wilson designated it so by executive order in 1916, and Congress made it official only in 1931 — and wouldn't be sung at a sporting event until the 1918 World Series. Not one of the 55 Mueller family contributions; Meissner was an unrelated contributor to the same volume.

title: In the Beginning
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Flett (Frieda's name in the Nickel household) began by expanding on Fred Knief's account of the early Muellers in Germany but soon ventured into speculation about Tante Caroline and her long relationship to the E.P. Wilhelm Mueller and Adelheid Rickmeyer (Frau Erica) household.

title: 19th-Century Life in Freedom Township (Pro)
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Life in Freedom Township, Minnesota, involved a lot of hard work in the first two decades of the 20th century, but Frieda found much of it fascinating and memorable.

title: 19th-Century Life in Freedom Township (Con)
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Although the happier elements of rural life are more easily remembered, rural life had many downsides not easily forgotten, including social isolation and very cold winters.

title: Hib and Addie's Early Days
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Frieda was a constant, very welcome, and helpful presence in her siblings' lives. She helped Hilbert and Adelheid from their windy wedding day, through the first one-room apartment, to young family life in a second-floor suburban flat, to the first family home on Ridgeland Avenue.

title: The Arrival of Joel
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Frieda was on hand as life grew far more complex with the first child and serious maternal health issues. She answered many early calls for help.

title: James: Birth and Maternal Thyroid Surgery
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Nothing went smoothly for the birth of the second child. Family life was complicated by a visiting grandparent's surgery, further maternal diabetes, thyroid surgery, and the baby's persistent colic. Frieda was there for it all.

title: Mark: A Quieter Arrival
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: In Frieda's telling, all of the troublesome maternal health and inter-generational problems seemed to have been set aside when the third son arrived. The death of [Opa Mueller](/documents/201), for whose geriatric and post-surgical care Frieda was summoned home, occurred a couple months before Mark arrived.

title: Thoughts on Retirement
author: Frieda Elisabeth Mueller
summary: Frieda's extended care-giver service for aging parents led to an LPN license and a late-in-life career as a charge nurse in the Lutheran Home for the Aged in Arlington Heights, Illinois. She moved to Illinois and her new career in the early 1960s.
